title: Remember, remember
hook: raam simar raam simar ihai tero kaaj hai: remember, this is your real work (Jaijavanti M9, ang 1352)

segments.voice: Yesterday, why search in the forest, and your line: scent in the flower. Did you stop to breathe once, right where you were? If the One is that close, what do we do about it? Today's hymn gives a job. Day five hundred eighty-five.
screen: `WHY SEARCH IN THE FOREST — SCENT IN THE FLOWER.`

segments.voice: Picture a to-do list on a Monday morning. Reply to the landlord. Book the dentist. Finish the report. Buy milk. Call Mom back. Return the package. It's long, and everything on it feels urgent. Now imagine someone gently taking the pen and writing one more line at the very top, above all of it, underlined twice. Not instead of the list. Above it. Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymn in Raag Jaijavanti does exactly that. It opens with a word said twice, and then says what your real work is.
screen: `A MONDAY TO-DO LIST.` → `ONE LINE WRITTEN AT THE TOP.` → `A WORD SAID TWICE.`

segments.voice: The hymn opens raam simar, raam simar, ihai tero kaaj hai. Remember the Lord, remember the Lord: this is your work. Simar is the root of simran, remembering, keeping the Lord in mind, often through repeating the Name. Raam, in Gurbani, is the all-pervading One. And kaaj is work, a task, the job you came to do. Why say it twice? Think of how you call someone who's drifting off: hey, hey. The doubling is a nudge, a hand on the shoulder. Then the hymn, in paraphrase: leave the company of maya, and take shelter with the Lord. Know the world's pleasures to be false; all this show is passing. Know wealth as a dream; why be proud of it? The kingdom of the whole earth, it says, is like a wall of sand. And near the end, Nanak says the body will perish, as time slips away moment by moment. Here's the surprising part. The hymn doesn't call remembering a hobby, or a reward for when the work is done. It calls it the work. Sikhs hear the same thought in a hymn of Guru Arjan's that's part of the evening prayer: no other task will help you; join the holy company and meditate on the Name alone. So the list doesn't vanish. You still buy the milk and call your mother. But the line at the top changes the rest. Remembering first makes the other jobs lighter, because they are no longer carrying your whole worth. That's simran: the work under all the work.
screen: `RAAM SIMAR, RAAM SIMAR.` · `KAAJ: THE JOB YOU CAME TO DO.` · `WEALTH AS A DREAM, A WALL OF SAND.` · `THE WORK UNDER ALL THE WORK.` · then, large: `THIS IS YOUR WORK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do your real work first. Before you look at the list, the phone, or the inbox, sit for these two minutes. Breathe slowly. If you pray, you can repeat Waheguru quietly, once on each breath, the way Sikhs practice simran. If you don't, just come back, again and again, to the plain fact that you're here and alive. When the list starts calling, let it wait. It'll still be there. This first. The bell holds the time.
Remember. Raam simar, raam simar: Guru Tegh Bahadur says twice that remembering the Lord is your real work, the job under every other job.
Your line: this is your work. Today, write one line at the top of your list, above everything: remember. Then let the rest follow. Day five hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs begin the day with simran, repeating Waheguru, before Nitnem and the day's work; Guru Tegh Bahadur's Jaijavanti shabad 'raam simar raam simar' is sung in kirtan as a call to that practice.

pairs: work, the task you came to do

myth: the hymn calls remembering a reward for when the work is done
it calls remembering the work itself: ihai tero kaaj hai.
the hymn says the opening call twice
raam simar, raam simar: a nudge, a hand on the shoulder.
the hymn says to drop all ordinary duties
the list stays; remembering goes at the top and makes the rest lighter.

fork.setup: your to-do list is long and urgent. what does the Jaijavanti hymn say is your real work?
fork.reveal: raam simar, raam simar, ihai tero kaaj hai: remember the Lord, remember: this is your work.

original.note: Gurmukhi: simran, remembering, from the same root as the hymn's simar.

trapdoor: what you thought: remembering is something to do once the real work is finished.
what it means: the hymn says remembering is the real work, and everything else sits under it.
what a scholar hears: kaaj, purpose or task, echoes Guru Arjan's line in the evening prayer that no other task will help you; the ninth Guru restates the fifth Guru's teaching in his own plain words.

sources.ref: Raag Jaijavanti, Mahalla 9, 'raam simar raam simar ihai tero kaaj hai' (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1352)

notes: Paraphrase of the Jaijavanti shabad (raam simar raam simar ihai terai kaaj hai; maaiaa ko sang tiaag prabh joo kee saran laag; jagat sukh maan mithiaa jhootho sabh saaj hai; supne jio dhan pachhaan kaahe par karat maan; baaroo kee bheet jaise basudhaa ko raaj hai; naanak jan kahat baat binas jaihai tero gaat chhin chhin kar gaio kaal ...): please confirm wording, especially the closing line, and Ang 1352.
The Rehras link (Asa M5, avar kaaj terai kitai na kaam, mil saadhsangat bhaj keval naam, Ang 12) should be confirmed.
